Rare disease Kids

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
They not even 16 yet and they have lived most of their lives knowing they have a are disease that may never be curable

Further information:
Rare disease kids
Heather Botha
She wanted to be a dancer, but now she is wheel chair bound.
In 2018 14 year old Heather Botha was diagnosed with a rare disease called Complex Regional Pain Syndrome or CRPS. Basically Sounds cause her pain. A simple sound like birds chirping can send her into a spiral of maddening pain. It first attacked her hand, but after a few months she regained the use of her hand and now it has attacked her feet. She is currently wheelchair bound, she describes the pain in her feet like walking on hot coals. There is no cure for CRPS so for now Heather cannot live a normal life. She has to constantly be protected from loud noises and pretty much says she is in pain almost all the time.

Dr Katinka van der Merwe, a South African specialist that practises in Arkansas, USA and treats patients with CRPS from all over the world using her neurologic recovery plan is the families last hope. She has an amazing track record of recovered patients that can cope better with this rare disorder. But she costs 500k and the family just can’t afford it

Constantly in pain – The nerves are out of sync and the sound vibrations make her in pain

Reece Trumpelmann
Reece was 11 when he was Diagnosed with an extremely rare disease called Gorlin-Glotz Syndrome, It is a syndrome that basically increases your chances of getting cancerous and non-cancerous tumours

In the past 4 years, since diagnosis, he has undergone 19 operations to remove 40 tumours from his jaw as well as various skin cancer all over his body. He has also had to have a bone graph, lost 16 teeth and had 5 dental plates

Reece is one of 3 people in SA with the condition. Due to a lack of knowledge locally, all they can do for him is treat the symptoms. There is one drug created to treat cancer that is available in the USA, which has shown promising results for long term treatment but again this family can’t afford to go to the USA for treatment.

Boikoketso Magana
Boikokoketso has xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) a rare disease that means she suffers the most extreme burns from sun exposure as as well as a much higher chance of getting skin cancer. Children with this condition are called twilight children. She was diagnosed when she was 5 years old, she is now 10 and can only leave the house at night. She does attend a normal school, but all she wants to do is play outside with her friends and she can’t.
She is 1 of 20 children in South Africa with the condition.

There is no treatment for this disease, Boikokoketso just has to stay out of the sun completely

Video of Iman
me and my cousin were jumping And he came down with his elbow into my face and it's just came that was the first one. And it swelled up And a few weeks later, they diagnosed me.
Heather: It's like. Being lit on fire
In South Africa there are an estimated 3.7 million people living with a rare disease and 50% of those are children. When a child is diagnosed with a disease that most doctors don’t know about, most medical aids won’t cover and most treatments aren’t available in South Africa they immediately have to become warriors and their mothers often become their doctors, nurses and advocacy experts
Marsha: 90 percent of the doctors And then they'll do their little bit of testing and then they'll refer you to the next specialist and the next specialist, refer you to the next specialist.
Reece trumpelman is one of three South Africans diagnosed with a genetic disease called Gorlin-Glotz syndrome. It increases his risk of developing various cancerous and non-cancerous tumours. Soon after his diagnoses his mom mARSHA quite her job to stay home and take care of Reece
3”upsound of her dressing his wounds
Marsha
we're battling with the skin cancers, we're battling with the tumors in the jaw, even though they're benign, they're extremely aggressive just eats away at his bones.
He has had over 40 tumours removed from his jaw
Reece: they basically explained to us that throughout my life, these things are going to keep growing. And every few months I would have to go in to get them removed.
When Heather Botha was 11 years old she had an accident that damaged the nerves in her hand, THAT never healed. After taking heather from specialist to specialist one doctor diagnosed her with a chronic pain disease called COMPLEX Regional PAIN SYNDROME.
Heather
Even talking about the pain makes it painful,
I want to scream into my pillow
With CRPS the damage to the nervous system makes pain occur spontaneously from any sensory stimulus and it is disproportionately more painful than it should be. Basically the nervous system keeps telling the body it is extreme pain
Heather:
majority of the pain is in her feet. She also has in her midsection area and then her hands as well.
audio stimuli is the worst for heather, the sound of a dog barking or a door slamming causes her nervous system to go into a pain response. On the MCGill pain scale CRPS can register as a 42 out of 50 which means is it more painful that having your finger amputated without anaesthesia
we have to, like, shut him in a little bubble, basically the only way that we can deal with the pain is to. Buffer, anything that makes the pain worse. literally lives in hell It's like watching your child burn
At 9 months old Iman casoojee was diagnosed with Spinal muscular atrophy 1, where the SNM1 gene that is vital to producing muscle building protein is absent and so the muscles atrophy or waste away
TASMEEN:
it affects your it affects your breathing muscles. It affects your ability to move, to walk, to set, to crawl. basically there was a time bomb in her life. you know that as the clock is ticking, the muscles are wasting away and you've got limited time with your child.
Even though there was no treatment at the time Iman’s family, with her mom Tasmin Jadwat at the helm, decided that they weren’t going to just sit down and wait for IMAN to die they were going to travel, find a specialist and live
Upsound from IMAN in the plane
So while they told us that there's nothing you can do here in America, they were saying that you need to manage the symptoms.
In order to try and prevent more tumours from forming Marsha has had to stop reece from doing a lot of things he loves, because every bump or knock can cause reece’s body to grow a tumour \
as parents we completely secluded because we've had to protect him. We've had to make sure that He doesn't get hurt.
eventhough it’s dangerous, off road biking is one thing Reece won’t give up. It’s the one thing he can do with his sisters that makes him feel normal
Claire: When you go riding does your mom not freak out a little in her heart
Reece: She makes me put on all the pads, everything. She doesn't come and watch us. Right, no matter where we go.
Before she got sick Heather loved to dance and sing and put on shows for her family, she had just started gymnastics and wanted to compete professional one day
If I wasn’t in this much pain and not in a wheelchair, I would be doing cartwheels and I just irritated my parents and always had to say, look at me, look at me, look at this cartwheel.
Every time I think about
That I used to. do that it Makes me sad
There is no cure for Reeces Gorlin-glotz but there is one treatment that can slow it down, but at the moment it is only available overseas
It's a chemo tablet which slows it down.
At what cost? 7000 U.S. dollars a month. For 30 tablets.
For the rest of his life, basically yes
The trumplemanns are fundraising and exploring every avenue possible to get Reece to the USA for treatment
obviously the surge is never going to stop. But my wish is that they can just slow down because then I've got more time to spend time with my friends, all of that.
4 years ago the first treatment for SMA was approved by the food and drug administration.
with this treatment what happens is that muscle protein that we need can be built up and she can regain some of the strength she's lost
At this point the costs are beyond anything this family can afford and their medical aid will not cover it, as SMA is not on the prescribed minimum benefits list
iman: Medical aids are putting a price tag on my life
Heather has tried almost every treatment in South Africa, including a program at the state's Red Cross War Memorial Children's Hospital’s pain management clinic, where she left able to walk but in a few months she was back in her wheelchair. Although this treatment did not work for Heather it has worked for many other CRPS patients across Africa
Heather believes the only hope left for her is a program in the united states created by South African ex-pat DR, Katinka Van De Merwe
As a child know that you are so incrediably brave knowing that you wake up in the morning, No one from the outside can understand the pain that you're going through.
Even doctors when they look at you, they're going to think you're overexaggerating your pain.
They have no concept of the fact that you feel like you're burned alive
But we've seen it. we've seen people in our community taking their own lives. We believe you
Dr VAN DER MERWE has agreed to only charge Heather 10% of the actual treatment costs and the family are doing everything they can to raise the funds to get her to America
you just have to come in willing to work very, very hard to see if your life depends on it, because it. That's right.
Iman turns 12 next year and even though her disease continues to diminish her muscle mass, she is determined to live life in spite of SMA
BIRTHDAY VIDEO – 5”
Iman has given us so much of joy over the years. She's been an inspiration to so many, teaching them not just about her condition, but how to accept people that are differently abled.
With the help of her mom, Iman has managed to tell her story around the world.
IMAN: Being different means you need to make A DIFFERENCE
